title: Tata Trusts to take Tata Sons to court over Chandrasekaran's reappointment as chairman
dek: The two main Tata trusts voted 3-2 to challenge the board's use of a casting vote and to seek ₹65 crore in damages, days before a Tata Sons board meeting on listing the group's holding company.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Tata Trusts, which together own about 66% of Tata Sons, the holding company of the Tata Group, have authorised legal action in the Bombay High Court against the reappointment of N. Chandrasekaran as Tata Sons chairman, escalating a boardroom dispute at the top of India's largest business group.

The Sir Dorabji Tata Trust and the Sir Ratan Tata Trust passed circular resolutions on Wednesday, 25 November, authorising the suits, according to reports. Each resolution passed 3-2: Noel Tata, the trusts' chairman, and Neville Tata voted in favour in both, joined by Bhaskar Bhat in the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust and by Maya Tata in the Sir Ratan Tata Trust, while Venu Srinivasan and Vijay Singh voted against, according to reports. Reports differed on whether the suits had been formally filed by Thursday.

## What the trusts want

The trusts are challenging the Tata Sons board's decision of 17 September approving Mr Chandrasekaran for a further five-year term from February 2027, and have named Tata Sons and six of its directors as defendants, according to reports. They are seeking:

- a declaration that the reappointment is invalid;
- an injunction barring Tata Sons from acting on the decision, or from passing resolutions without the affirmative votes required by its Articles of Association, including by using a casting vote on contested items;
- damages of ₹65 crore, ₹50 crore for the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust and ₹15 crore for the Sir Ratan Tata Trust, with 18% annual interest, according to reports.

The trusts want interim relief before a Tata Sons board meeting rescheduled to Monday, 30 November, whose agenda is expected to include the proposed listing of Tata Sons, a corporate reorganisation and shareholder approval for the reappointment, according to reports.

## The casting-vote dispute

The disagreement turns on Article 121 of Tata Sons' Articles of Association, which the trusts say requires key board decisions to have the affirmative votes of a majority of the directors nominated by the trusts. At the 17 September meeting, the board voted 4-1 for the reappointment, with Mr Chandrasekaran recusing himself, according to reports. The two trust nominees split: Noel Tata voted against and Venu Srinivasan in favour. Independent director Harish Manwani, chairing the item, then used a casting vote in favour.

The trusts argue that a casting vote "can only break a tie at the board level" and cannot override disagreement between the two nominee directors, and have called the reappointment illegal. Legal opinions obtained earlier from former Supreme Court judges B.N. Srikrishna and U.U. Lalit backed the casting vote as valid under the Articles, according to reports. Tata Sons has said the minutes of the meeting were circulated and revised to include Noel Tata's comments; he has since sought recordings and records of how his objections were handled, according to reports. Tata Sons had not commented publicly on the planned suit by Thursday afternoon.

## Why it matters

Tata Sons controls listed companies including Tata Consultancy Services, Tata Motors, Tata Steel and Titan, so a court fight between its controlling shareholders and its board is an unusual governance risk for investors in the group. The dispute is also tied to the question of whether Tata Sons should list its own shares to meet Reserve Bank of India rules for large non-bank financial companies, which Tata Sons is preparing for and the trusts oppose, according to reports.

The Venu Srinivasan family is separately in a dispute of its own: his daughter Lakshmi Venu has filed a suit seeking partition of the family's assets, according to reports.
